evaluated.name: LossFirmInventoryBuildup
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory accumulation is benign for profitable firms but signals unsold output, demand misjudgment, and impending write-downs when the firm is already generating losses; the market underreacts to this joint signal.
evaluated.reasoning: Working-capital investment (invt growth) alone is a weak predictor, but conditioned on negative profitability (low ib/at) it becomes a forced-inventory / distressed-liquidation indicator rather than a demand-anticipation indicator. Ranking both legs keeps the interaction scale-free and lets the product isolate firms that are simultaneously in the top of buildup and the top of unprofitability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ExternalFinancingGapLeverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(capx, at), RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose investment outlays exceed operating cash flow must fund the gap externally; when they are already highly levered, that funding is costly, dilutive, or rationed, so expected equity value is impaired relative to firms with the same gap but spare debt capacity.
evaluated.reasoning: The first leg measures the internal-funding shortfall of the investment program, the second measures the remaining balance-sheet capacity to close it. The economic content lies in their conjunction: a large gap is harmless with low leverage but is a solvency stressor at high leverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccumulatedLossExpansionIntensity
evaluated.hypothesis: Total expansion outlays (organic capex plus acquisitions) predict low returns in proportion to how deeply a firm has eroded its accumulated earnings base, because expansion funded from a depleted equity cushion reflects gambling for resurrection rather than reinvestment of internally generated profit.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the binary negative-retained-earnings switch with a continuous rank of NEG(re/at) removes the large mass of firms tied at exactly zero, so every quintile is populated by a genuine gradient of cumulative-loss depth rather than by an arbitrary composition of the zero group. Industry-ranking the expansion leg strips out mechanical differences in capital intensity, so the interaction isolates firms investing aggressively relative to peers precisely when their retained-earnings cushion is most depleted.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtFundedInvestmentEscalation
evaluated.hypothesis: Increases in investment intensity are value-destroying when they are simultaneously accompanied by a deteriorating liability ratio (debt-funded escalation of commitment), whereas the same investment increase financed while deleveraging reflects genuine internal cash generation and is not penalized.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the two-sided ACCEL term with a bounded rank of the change in capex intensity ensures that investment *decelerators* sit near zero instead of dominating the negative tail, resolving the sign contradiction the critic identified. Replacing the binary leverage indicator with a winsorized z-score of the change in lt/at removes the half-sample zero mass and orders the funding channel continuously, so the extreme long leg is populated by firms raising investment while deleveraging and the extreme short leg by firms raising investment while levering up.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MaturityMismatchedCapitalDeepening
evaluated.hypothesis: Building long-lived physical capital while running a negative working-capital position is a maturity mismatch: illiquid, slow-payback assets are being funded by claims that come due within a year, so any refinancing friction forces distressed asset sales.
evaluated.reasoning: The mechanism is not the level of leverage but the *term structure* of the funding relative to the term structure of the assets, which is why the fragility leg uses current liabilities net of current assets rather than total debt. Gross PPE growth is the cleanest measure of long-duration commitment, and the interaction predicts poor returns only for the mismatched corner while liquid capital-deepeners are unpenalized.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftCollateralLeverage
evaluated.hypothesis: The expected cost of financial distress depends on asset redeployability: leverage carried against intangible, non-collateralizable assets implies far lower recovery values and steeper fire-sale discounts than the same leverage against tangible capital, and the market underprices this heterogeneity in distress cost.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests a mechanism no archive signal touches — the *composition* of accumulated investment rather than its rate — by asking whether past investment produced pledgeable or unpledgeable assets. Using lt/(lt+ceq) rather than lt/at avoids double-counting the intangible asset base in the denominator of the leverage leg, so the two legs measure genuinely separate quantities.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OverHiringUnderLeverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Headcount growth that outruns revenue growth embeds rigid, hard-to-reverse operating costs; combined with high financial leverage this compounds operating and financial leverage, raising the probability that a modest demand shock becomes a solvency event.
evaluated.reasoning: Labor is the investment margin with the highest adjustment cost, and benchmarking it against contemporaneous sales growth isolates genuine over-expansion from capacity that demand has already justified. The interaction with total leverage captures the classic combined-leverage mechanism, a different economic channel from funding deficits, and it uses a real-side fragility trigger that RMW and CMA do not span.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ForcedRetrenchmentFromCapexPeak
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(capx, at), 5), RATIO(capx, at))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital expenditure that has collapsed far below the firm's own five-year peak is disciplined retrenchment for a sound firm but a symptom of a credit-driven investment spiral for a levered one; forced underinvestment destroys franchise value that the low-investment premium would otherwise reward.
evaluated.reasoning: This directly adjudicates the "forced versus voluntary" question the archive has only asserted, using the firm's own investment history as the benchmark so that the shortfall is measured against its established scale rather than the cross-section. If the sign comes out positive instead, that is informative evidence that retrenchment is rewarded even under leverage and would redirect the whole search toward resilience rather than value destruction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ReinvestmentAgainstDebtServiceCapacity
evaluated.hypothesis: The relevant fragility constraint is not how much of the balance sheet creditors own but how many years of operating cash flow it would take to retire their claims; firms reinvesting rapidly into their installed capital base while cash-flow-to-total-debt is thin are expanding capacity they cannot service.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the deficit-difference structure of the archive signal entirely: neither leg is a funding gap, and the fragility leg is Beaver's cash-flow-to-debt coverage ratio, a flow-versus-obligation solvency measure rather than a stock leverage ratio, so a low-leverage firm with weak cash conversion is now flagged while an asset-heavy but cash-generative one is not. The investment leg is the reinvestment rate on installed capital (capx/ppent), which measures capacity expansion relative to the firm's own productive base rather than relative to total assets, so neither leg replicates the earlier construct or the accruals anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtFundedAcquisitionProgram
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, 0), 3), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(lt, at), LAG(RATIO(lt, at), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A multi-year acquisition program that has been accompanied by a rising liability ratio identifies roll-ups that bought growth with creditors' money; integration risk and overpayment are then compounded by a balance sheet that has been permanently weakened, whereas acquirers who levered down while buying were paying from genuine surplus.
evaluated.reasoning: This removes the sstk/oancf leg that collapsed into a cash-profitability sort and replaces it with the *joint three-year trajectory* of acquisition spending and leverage, so the signal fires only when the external-financing evidence and the expansion evidence line up over the same multi-year window rather than in a single noisy fiscal year. Cumulating aqc over three years with unreported acquisitions treated as zero gives a continuous, well-populated program-intensity measure, and the matched three-year leverage change identifies the funding source directly rather than assuming it.

evaluated.name: FundingGapVsLiquidityBuffer
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(capx, at), RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: An investment program that outruns operating cash flow is dangerous in proportion to how little cash the firm holds against claims falling due within the year; the binding constraint is the near-term liquidity buffer, not the long-run stock of debt.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one design choice against the best archive signal — swapping the debt/assets conditioner for cash-to-current-liabilities — to test the diagnosis that flow-and-liquidity fragility, not stock leverage, is what generates a genuine raw spread rather than a loading-driven alpha. Cash-to-current-liabilities is also close to industry-neutral, so it should avoid the systematic sector bets that flattened the Sharpe of the leverage-conditioned signals.

evaluated.name: CapitalCommitmentUnderEarningsInstability
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility is not only a level of obligations but the volatility of the earnings stream that must service them; committing irreversible capital at a high rate when profitability has been historically unstable raises the probability that the investment matures into a state where cash flow cannot cover it.
evaluated.reasoning: This opens a second-moment fragility channel that no archive signal tests — distress risk proxied by realized earnings instability rather than balance-sheet ratios — and pairs it with the reinvestment rate on installed capital, the investment leg that already worked in ReinvestmentAgainstDebtServiceCapacity. Because earnings volatility is largely orthogonal to the value and profitability characteristics that manufacture FF5 loadings, any alpha here is less likely to be a repackaged factor bet.

evaluated.name: GoodwillStockWeakCashCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: A large stock of acquired goodwill represents past investment whose value depends entirely on delivered cash flow; when operating cash flow is thin relative to total obligations, that goodwill is an impairment and covenant risk rather than an asset, and equity holders bear the write-down.
evaluated.reasoning: This retains the collateral-quality channel that produced the largest archive alpha but replaces its leverage-level conditioner — which delivered a near-zero raw spread and a wrong-signed FMB slope — with the cash-coverage conditioner that worked in Family A, making it a direct test of whether the collateral mechanism survives once the factor-loading bet is removed. Treating unreported goodwill as zero is the economically correct convention (a firm with no acquisitions has no goodwill) and keeps coverage high.

evaluated.name: BufferDepletionFinancedInvestment
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is not that a funding gap exists but which pocket paid for it: firms whose capital spending coincides with a drawdown of their own cash reserves relative to obligations due within the year are consuming their last self-insurance, so the next adverse shock must be met in external markets on distressed terms.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the deficit-times-leverage structure entirely: the fragility leg is a *flow of internal liquidity being consumed*, scaled by near-term claims, rather than a stock of debt or a static buffer, so it identifies the realized funding source instead of inferring strain from the balance sheet. It also uses no oancf, so coverage should rise toward the 0.12 ceiling rather than sitting at the 0.09 of the oancf-based archive signals, letting us test whether the funding-strain channel survives on a substantially larger sample.

evaluated.name: ExpansionIntoContractingDemand
evaluated.hypothesis: Committing capital at a high rate while the revenue base is actually shrinking reveals management extrapolating a demand path the market has already stopped validating; the resulting capacity arrives into weak demand, producing fixed-cost drag and write-downs.
evaluated.reasoning:
Scaling capex by *lagged* net PP&E removes the mechanical feedback the critic identified — the current year's investment no longer enters the denominator — and replacing the turnover delta with raw sales growth makes the fragility leg a pure demand-side variable that is not constructed from any capital-stock quantity. The interaction is genuine because rapid reinvestment is unpenalized when revenue is growing and revenue contraction is unpenalized when the firm is not adding capacity, so the extreme tail is only the pro-cyclical over-builder.

evaluated.name: SectorAdjustedDeficitDistressScore
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUB(RATIO(capx, at), RATIO(oancf, at))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment shortfalls should be judged against sector norms for capital intensity, and fragility is better captured by a two-dimensional solvency-plus-liquidity score than by leverage alone; a firm is at risk when it out-spends its cash flow relative to industry peers while ranking poorly on both indebtedness and working-capital cushion.
evaluated.reasoning:
The industry adjustment is now applied to the *investment* leg, where the sector confound genuinely lives (capital intensity differs by an order of magnitude across industries), while the fragility leg is upgraded from a single leverage ratio to an Altman-flavoured composite of solvency and liquidity ranks — a substantive change of the conditioning variable, not an operator substitution. Both legs remain bounded and monotone in fragility, so the earlier problem of a signed conditioner pushing below-industry-leverage deficit firms into the long leg does not arise.

evaluated.name: ExpansionOnThinTangibleNetWorth
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(at, COALESCE(intan, 0)), lt), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Creditors and rating agencies evaluate solvency on a tangible-net-worth basis; a firm expanding aggressively while its assets net of intangibles barely cover — or fail to cover — its liabilities has no genuine equity cushion, so incremental investment is financed entirely by claimholders' forbearance.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the definition of fragility rather than the conditioner's data source: tangible net worth over assets is the covenant-relevant solvency measure and is systematically stricter than lt/at precisely for the acquisitive firms the archive leader flags, giving a sharper distinction between accounting equity and pledgeable equity. Both legs are continuous with high-coverage inputs, and the interaction is real because expansion is unpenalized when tangible equity is ample and thin tangible equity is unpenalized when the firm is not expanding.

evaluated.name: FreshGoodwillWeakCashCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: The value destruction lies in recently booked acquisition premia, not in long-seasoned goodwill: deals closed within the last three years have not yet been tested by an impairment cycle, so when cash coverage is weak the market has not yet marked down the price paid.
evaluated.reasoning: This decomposes the archive leader along the economically decisive dimension — vintage of the capitalized premium — by replacing the goodwill *stock* with the three-year *increment*, which is populated only by actual acquirers and therefore also mitigates the tied-zero-mass problem in the stock version. A stronger result would identify overpayment-and-impairment timing as the mechanism; a weaker one would show the effect resides in stale, chronically unproductive intangible-heavy balance sheets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TotalFundingRequirementBurden
evaluated.hypothesis: The credit-relevant quantity is the total cash the firm must raise in the coming year — capital expenditure it has committed to plus debt actually maturing, less what operations will generate — and equity in firms with a large required raise is exposed to whatever terms the market imposes.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the rank-product form entirely and builds the credit analyst's cash-flow-adequacy construct, in which the investment commitment and the maturing obligation enter the *same* numerator because they compete for the same dollars, something no product of two separately ranked legs can represent. It is not a relabeling of the archive leader: no intangible or goodwill quantity appears, the fragility content comes from debt in current maturities rather than a coverage ratio, and the additive structure lets a large maturity wall offset a modest capex program and vice versa.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RefinancingWallAgainstCommitment
evaluated.hypothesis: Rollover risk is distinct from solvency risk: a firm can have comfortable total-obligation coverage yet be unable to meet claims falling due within twelve months out of cash on hand plus one year of operations, and committing capital irreversibly against that near-term wall is what converts illiquidity into insolvency.
evaluated.reasoning:
The obligation horizon changes from total liabilities to claims maturing within the year, and the resource side becomes stock-plus-flow (cash reserves plus operating cash flow) rather than flow alone, so this measures liquidity coverage of a refinancing wall rather than long-run debt-service capacity — economically the difference between a liquidity crisis and a solvency problem. The archive already shows near-term liquidity conditioning produces a real raw spread (FundingGapVsLiquidityBuffer, Sharpe −0.40), but there the cash buffer was measured without the operating flow that actually replenishes it.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WithinLeverageInvestmentSmoothness
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms carrying heavy obligations, smooth reinvestment reveals spending planned from stable internal cash flow, while erratic stop-start investment reveals improvisation around financing windows; for unlevered firms the distinction carries no information because no creditor constraint binds.
evaluated.reasoning:
Centering the smoothness leg as a z-score while keeping leverage as a non-negative weight means both the long and short extremes are populated by *high-leverage* firms — smooth ones long, erratic ones short — so the leverage main effect largely nets out of the spread instead of being the whole of the long leg, which was the critic's objection. Low-leverage firms now sit near zero regardless of their investment volatility, making the test genuinely about investment-policy stability conditional on fragility.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtYearsOfRevenueExpansion
evaluated.hypothesis: Debt is ultimately serviced out of revenue, not out of book assets, so obligations measured in years of sales is the fragility metric that cannot be flattered by capitalized acquisition premia or asset write-ups; expanding capacity while owing many years of revenue is the value-destroying combination.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the mismeasured txt leg and replaces it with debt-to-revenue, which is not a profitability proxy at all — a highly profitable firm can owe many years of sales and a lossmaking one can owe few — so it cannot be a restatement of the investment × low-profitability interaction. Industry-ranking the fragility leg neutralizes the sector turnover differences that make raw debt-to-sales a utilities-and-real-estate bet, and because it needs no oancf, coverage should run near the 0.12 ceiling rather than the 0.09 of the cash-coverage family.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ShortTermClaimFinancedCapex
evaluated.hypothesis: When capital spending is accompanied by an expansion of claims due within twelve months — stretched payables, accrued liabilities, drawn revolvers — the firm is funding long-lived assets with the most fugitive form of finance, and any tightening forces liquidation at the worst moment.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates the *funding source actually used* through the contemporaneous flow of short-term claims, which is different from the archive's level-based maturity-mismatch signal and from the funding-gap family that only measures whether a shortfall exists without identifying who filled it. Both legs use high-coverage annual items, so it also provides a large-sample read on the maturity-structure mechanism that has so far only been tested on levels.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TangibleIntensityWeakCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: If weak cash coverage of obligations is the true source of the archive's leading results, then it should be equally damaging when the asset base is hard physical capital; if instead the effect requires unpledgeable capitalized premia, tangible-asset intensity should attenuate or reverse it because property supports both borrowing and recovery.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a deliberate identification control for the two strongest signals: it holds the cash-coverage conditioner fixed and swaps the investment-stock leg from goodwill to its economic opposite, tangible plant. A strongly negative result would show the coverage leg does the work and the goodwill framing is decoration, redirecting the last generations toward pure coverage-based constructs; a weak result would establish asset redeployability as the essential second ingredient and justify concentrating on intangible-heavy expansion.

evaluated.name: TotalCashUsesRequirement
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash a firm must find in the coming year is the sum of *all* investment uses — fixed capital plus the working capital absorbed by inventory — plus debt actually maturing, less what operations generate; for expanding firms the inventory build is often the larger and less discretionary of the two investment uses.
evaluated.reasoning:
Every term is now a flow measured over the same fiscal year, so the stock-versus-flow inconsistency disappears and the signal cannot become a disguised cash-holdings sort. Broadening the investment definition to include working-capital absorption is a substantive economic claim about which outlays compete for the same dollars — and it connects the archive's two independent successes, the funding-requirement construct and the loss-firm inventory buildup result (fmb −2.76), inside a single budget identity rather than as a rank product.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: InflexibleCapexUnderFundingNeed
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(capx, ppent), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A funding requirement is survivable if the firm can simply stop spending; it becomes distress when the capital program is irreducible. A firm whose own five-year minimum reinvestment rate is high has demonstrated it cannot operate below a costly maintenance floor, so it must go to the market on whatever terms are offered.
evaluated.reasoning:
The conditioning variable is investment *inflexibility* — the firm's revealed floor on reinvestment, taken from its own time series — which is a new construct in this archive and is economically orthogonal to collateral quality and to the level of cash coverage that drives the goodwill result, so a strong outcome is informative about a distinct mechanism rather than a restatement. The interaction is genuine in both directions: a large required raise is manageable for a firm that can idle its capital budget, and a high maintenance floor is harmless for a firm generating surplus cash.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NearTermCashUsesNetOfLiquidAssets
evaluated.hypothesis: Total near-term cash needs are the capital program plus the amount by which claims due within a year exceed the liquid assets available to settle them; firms scoring high on this combined measure must either raise money or cut investment under duress.
evaluated.reasoning:
This eliminates the double-counting error — dlc no longer appears separately because it sits inside lct exactly once — and the netting is now internally consistent, current claims against current assets. Because it requires no cash-flow-statement data, it extends the funding-requirement mechanism from the 0.09-coverage post-1988 sample to roughly the 0.13 ceiling, and its additive structure is a different object from the archive's rank-product maturity-mismatch signal, in which capital spending never entered.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LongDurationAssetsShortDatedDebt
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility comes from the mismatch between how long a firm's assets take to return cash and how soon its claims come due: heavy long-lived plant funded by a liability structure concentrated in current maturities means the firm must refinance repeatedly against assets it cannot sell quickly.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the equity-cushion leg whose sign was confounded by share repurchases and replaces it with the *composition* of the debt structure — the share of obligations that is short-dated — which is not a leverage level and therefore avoids the factor-loading artifact that has plagued lt/at conditioners. It is also distinct from the accepted flow-based short-term-claim signal: here nothing is changing, the point is that the standing balance-sheet duration gap is itself the risk, and both legs use high-coverage annual items.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: EarningsBasedCashUses
evaluated.hypothesis: If the funding-requirement effect works through genuine cash scarcity, replacing realized operating cash flow with accrual earnings should weaken it, because accrual earnings can be reported while the cash never arrives; if the effect survives intact, the mechanism is broader financial strain rather than liquidity specifically.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a deliberate identification test between the two candidate generation terms, motivated by the archive's sharpest result — removing the generation term entirely destroyed the FMB slope while leaving the alpha intact — so establishing *which* generation measure matters is the highest-value remaining question. It has a second payoff: because ib is available for the full sample, a surviving result would extend the leading mechanism from 0.082 coverage to roughly the 0.13 ceiling and to the pre-1988 period, materially strengthening the evidence base rather than merely restating it.

evaluated.name: AgingCapitalWeakCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: A heavily depreciated capital stock represents deferred, non-discretionary future investment: the replacement wave is coming whether or not the firm can afford it, and a firm carrying old assets alongside weak cash coverage of its obligations faces a capital-spending obligation it must fund on distressed terms.
evaluated.reasoning: Capital vintage measured as accumulated depreciation over gross plant is a stock construct the archive has never used, and it is conceptually the opposite of the investment-flow legs: it identifies firms that have *under*-invested and now owe the catch-up, which the low-investment premium would otherwise reward. Pairing it with cash coverage tests whether the market distinguishes voluntary capital discipline from an unfunded replacement liability — precisely the "forced versus disciplined" question the brief poses and that the archive's retrenchment signals answered only ambiguously.

evaluated.name: NoHeadroomFundingNeed
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(RATIO(lt, at), TS_MAX(RATIO(lt, at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm needing external funds can absorb the shock if it still has room under its own demonstrated debt ceiling; a firm already sitting at the highest leverage it has carried in five years has exhausted the capacity its lenders and covenants tolerate, so the required raise must come from equity or from asset sales.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner is leverage relative to the firm's *own* five-year maximum rather than the cross-sectional leverage level, which is the specific change that should avoid the factor-loading artifact — utilities and other structurally levered firms sit mid-range on this measure, while a normally conservative firm that has just levered to a record scores at the top. This makes debt-capacity exhaustion, not indebtedness, the fragility concept, and it interacts with the requirement in exactly the way the mechanism predicts: headroom is irrelevant when no money is needed.

evaluated.name: HiringAgainstWeakCashCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Headcount growth is an unfunded, hard-to-reverse cash commitment that never appears in the capital budget; adding payroll when operating cash flow is thin relative to obligations creates a fixed claim that competes with debt service and must be unwound through costly layoffs.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests the labor margin — the one investment channel entirely outside the cash-budget identity the leading signals exploit — using the cash-coverage conditioner that has produced real raw spreads, rather than the leverage level that made the archive's earlier hiring signal a loading artifact (fmb +0.92, Sharpe −0.065). If it works, it demonstrates the fragility mechanism generalizes beyond balance-sheet cash uses to operating commitments, which would be genuinely new evidence rather than a refinement.

evaluated.name: FundingStrainSurprise
evaluated.expression: RANK(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Chronically cash-hungry business models are understood and priced by the market, whereas a firm whose funding requirement has just jumped above its own recent norm presents information investors have not yet incorporated; the return predictability should come from the innovation in strain, not its level.
evaluated.reasoning: This distinguishes a persistent characteristic from a state change on the archive's strongest construct — if the deviation-from-own-norm version retains the FMB slope, the effect is genuine underreaction to new strain, while if it collapses the effect is a stable risk characteristic, and either answer determines how the final generations should be spent. It is not a horizon rescaling of the level signal: benchmarking against the firm's own three-year average removes exactly the cross-sectional variation that the level version ranks on.

evaluated.name: IlliquidWorkingCapitalWeakCoverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms with identical current ratios differ enormously in real liquidity depending on whether their current assets are cash and receivables or unsold inventory; when operating cash flow is already thin relative to obligations, a working-capital position locked up in goods that only convert at fire-sale discounts is the difference between a manageable squeeze and a forced liquidation.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the deflator-swap framing entirely and tests the *composition* of liquid resources rather than their quantity — a channel the archive has never examined, since every prior liquidity conditioner (che/lct, act−lct, che+oancf over lct) treats all current assets as equivalent claims-paying capacity. The interaction is economically necessary in both directions: heavy inventory is a normal, financeable business model for a firm generating cash, and weak coverage is far more survivable when current assets are already near-cash, so neither leg carries the prediction alone.

evaluated.name: TotalCorporateCashUses
evaluated.expression: RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), DELTA(invt, 1)), dlc), oancf), at))
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquisitions are a discretionary cash use that competes for the same dollars as capital expenditure and debt repayment, and the archive's goodwill results imply acquisitive firms with weak cash generation are the most exposed, so cash spent on deals belongs inside the funding requirement rather than outside it.

evaluated.name: RequirementWithLockedUpWorkingCapital
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(invt, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that must raise money can bridge the gap from its own current assets only if those assets are near-cash; if its liquidity is locked in inventory that converts slowly and at a discount, the same requirement forces it into the external market or into a fire sale.

evaluated.name: NonDiscretionaryCashUses

considered.name: RequirementWithFallingLaborProductivity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(sale, emp), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Deteriorating revenue per employee means the existing workforce is no longer earning its keep, so a firm in that state which also needs outside cash faces the same operating-cost rigidity as an over-hirer, without having hired anyone.
considered.reasoning: This tests the labor-rigidity mechanism through productivity rather than through headcount growth, which matters because the accepted hiring version overlaps the published hiring-rate anomaly and its result could be attributed to that known effect rather than to the conjunction. Falling sales per employee is not a documented standalone predictor in the same way, so a comparable result here would attribute the amplification to operating-cost rigidity rather than to a repackaged labor-investment anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementWithSelfBenchmarkedOverhang
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5))
considered.hypothesis: The right benchmark for an inventory overhang may be the firm's own operating policy rather than its industry: a firm currently holding more days of stock than at any point in its own five-year history has accumulated goods relative to how it normally runs, and that accumulation is unconvertible exactly when outside cash is needed.
considered.reasoning:
This is a competing-benchmark hypothesis rather than a coverage splice: industry ranking controls for technology across firms, while own-history ranking controls for it within the firm and additionally purges the permanent component that makes the peer-relative version overlap the published inventory-level anomaly. Comparing it against the archived peer-benchmarked result cleanly identifies whether the amplifier is a cross-sectional characteristic or a firm-specific deviation, which is the substantive question left open by the leading signal.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CenteredOverhangConditionalRequirement
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(invt, sale)))
considered.hypothesis: A funding requirement should be penalized when the firm carries more inventory than its industry peers and rewarded when it carries less, because lean, convertible stock means the cash need reflects growth the firm can finance from its own operating cycle rather than accumulation it cannot.
considered.reasoning:
The sign inconsistency is removed by keeping the requirement leg as a non-negative bounded rank and centering only the amplifier: firms with no funding need sit near zero regardless of inventory, high-need firms with above-peer stock populate the short leg, and high-need firms with below-peer stock populate the long leg, exactly as the hypothesis states. This is a genuinely different conditional structure from every archived rank product, in which below-peer-inventory firms with large needs were forced into the middle of the sort rather than onto the favourable side.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OverhangInclusiveFundingRequirement
considered.expression: RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), MUL(sale, IND_ADJ(RATIO(invt, sale)))), at))
considered.hypothesis: Abnormal inventory is not merely a symptom that amplifies a cash need — it is itself capital the firm has already committed and must continue to finance, so the dollar value of stock held beyond the industry norm belongs inside the funding requirement rather than beside it.
considered.reasoning:
Converting the peer-relative overhang into dollars (sales multiplied by abnormal inventory days) and adding it to the cash-uses identity is a different construction from any rank product: it lets a large overhang offset a comfortable cash position and vice versa, imposing an economic exchange rate between the two quantities instead of requiring both to be extreme. This also avoids the blend criticism entirely, since nothing is being averaged — the amplifier enters the budget constraint as a financing need with its own units.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OverhangFundedByMaturingDebt
considered.hypothesis: Excess inventory is dangerous when it has been financed with debt that comes due before the goods can be sold: the firm must convert stock into cash on the creditor's timetable rather than the customer's, which is the classic setup for a discounted liquidation.
considered.reasoning:
This replaces the trivial standalone ratio with a genuine two-sided interaction between the working-capital overhang and the maturity of the claims financing it, so it cannot be read as the published inventory-level anomaly, and it tests whether the inventory channel operates through refinancing timing rather than through demand expectations. It also requires no cash-flow-statement data, giving coverage near the 0.13 ceiling — valuable because every leading archive signal is confined to roughly 8% coverage.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementWithTradeCreditTightening
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), sale), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Suppliers and other operating creditors react to deteriorating prospects before capital markets do; when the non-debt current liabilities a firm carries per dollar of sales contract, its trade counterparties are shortening terms, and a firm that simultaneously needs outside cash has lost its cheapest and most flexible funding source.
considered.reasoning:
Subtracting current debt from current liabilities isolates the payables-and-accruals component that the trade-credit story actually concerns, which removes both the revolver-repayment confound and the mechanical overlap with the dlc term in the requirement leg. The amplifier now reflects the behaviour of external operating claimholders rather than the firm's own commitments, making it economically distinct from the inventory and labor conditioners tested so far.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OwnHistoryOverhangInclusiveRequirement
considered.expression: RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), MUL(sale, SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), TS_MIN(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)))), at))
considered.hypothesis: Inventory held above the leanest level the firm has itself demonstrated it can operate at is capital that has been committed without necessity, and those dollars belong inside the funding requirement alongside capital spending and maturing debt because they must be financed until the goods clear.
considered.reasoning: This unites the round's two strongest findings in the one combination not yet run — the dollarized budget-identity structure that produced alpha −5.9% and the own-history benchmark that produced alpha −6.5% — but it is not a rank splice: the overhang enters in dollars against the firm's own demonstrated minimum, so a modest cash need with a severe self-relative stock build ranks alongside a large cash need with lean stock. Benchmarking against the firm's own five-year minimum rather than the industry mean also purges the permanent technology component that makes peer-relative inventory overlap the published inventory-level anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BroadSampleSelfBenchmarkedOverhang
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), dlc), ib), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5))
considered.hypothesis: If the leading result reflects a genuine financing constraint rather than a feature of the post-1988 cash-flow-statement subsample, it must survive when accrual earnings measure internal funds, on a sample half again as large and covering the earlier decades.
considered.reasoning: Every top signal in this archive rests on roughly 8% coverage, which is its single binding weakness, and the earnings-based requirement has already been shown to retain full cross-sectional predictability at 0.119 coverage (t = −4.85) when paired with the turnover conditioner. The success criterion here is comparability rather than a higher score: a materially weaker wide-sample result would mean the mechanism is period-specific and the narrow-sample leader should be discounted accordingly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementWithLaborOverhang
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(emp, sale), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Firms accumulate unfunded commitments in people exactly as they do in goods: a headcount that is high relative to revenue by the firm's own historical standard is an overhang of fixed cash claims, and it binds hardest when the firm already needs outside money.
considered.reasoning: This ports the winning own-history benchmark from the working-capital margin to the labor margin, which is a substantively different commitment — payroll never appears in the cash-budget identity and cannot be liquidated at a discount — and it improves on the archive's hiring-growth conditioner by measuring the *level* of overstaffing relative to the firm's own norm rather than the one-year change. Because the benchmark is the firm's own history, it is distinct from the published hiring-rate anomaly, which is a cross-sectional growth sort.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementWithCapacityOverhang
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(ppent, sale), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Fixed capacity carried above the firm's own historical revenue-adjusted norm is idle plant: it generates depreciation and maintenance obligations without sales, and a firm needing external cash cannot convert it quickly except at a liquidation discount.
considered.reasoning: This completes the test of whether own-history overhang is a general concept spanning all three asset margins — working capital, labor and fixed capital — or is specific to inventory, which matters for interpreting the leading signal as a financing-constraint mechanism rather than an inventory-anomaly variant. It also revisits the capital margin with a construction that succeeded elsewhere, after the earlier vintage-based attempt (accumulated depreciation over gross plant) produced a flat cross-sectional slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementWithDepletedOwnLiquidity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), TS_RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct)), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Cash-to-short-term-claims is a firm-specific policy variable, so what signals strain is not a low level but a level low by the firm's own standard: a firm whose liquidity buffer sits at the bottom of its five-year range while it faces a funding requirement has already spent its self-insurance.
considered.reasoning: Earlier cross-sectional cash-buffer conditioners either failed on the FMB slope or risked rediscovering the published cash-to-assets anomaly, and the own-history benchmark is precisely the fix, since it differences out the firm's permanent cash policy and isolates depletion. It closes the batch with the one fragility dimension that is neither a commitment nor an asset overhang but the exhaustion of the reserve that would otherwise absorb the requirement.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RequirementWithMultiYearStockBuild
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, dlc), oancf), at)), RANK(TREND(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose inventory days have been drifting upward year after year has a structural accumulation problem — goods entering faster than they clear, over multiple demand cycles — which is a different and more damaging state than a single high reading, and it leaves the firm least able to self-fund when cash is needed.
considered.reasoning:
The amplifier is the five-year *slope* of inventory days rather than the current position within that window, so it is directional and chronic rather than a level measured on a different scale: a firm sitting at the top of its range after a sharp one-year build scores high on TS_RANK but low on TREND, while a firm three years into a steady drift scores the reverse. This uses the one temporal construct the archive has never tested, and it discriminates a genuine economic question left open by the leading signal — whether the overhang that matters is an acute spike or a persistent multi-year deterioration in how fast the firm converts stock into cash.
REASONING_END
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: The loss-conditioning of inventory buildup is an economically sensible twist and the rank-product direction matches the negative expected sign, but the signal is close to a mechanical product of two documented effects (inventory-growth accruals-style predictability and low profitability), so much of any FF5 alpha risks being absorbed by RMW/CMA and the incremental interaction content must be demonstrated against the two standalone legs.

The conditional story is coherent and correctly signed, but because capx/at is non-negative and the indicator zeroes out the large majority of firms, most of the cross-section is tied at exactly zero, leaving ill-defined middle/long quintiles and a spread whose sign is driven by the arbitrary composition of the zero mass rather than by the hypothesized interaction.

The internal-funding-shortfall leg times remaining debt capacity is a genuine conjunction with a clear mechanism and a direction that matches the negative expected sign; the main caveats are oancf-driven coverage loss (post-1988) and the need to show the interaction beats the additive financing-deficit and leverage legs.

The expression is internally inconsistent with the hypothesis because asset growth is signed: dividing by a small current ratio makes sharply *shrinking* illiquid firms the most extreme negative values, so the low end of the sort is contaminated by contractions rather than isolating unfunded expansion, and winsorization only masks rather than fixes the near-zero-denominator instability.

ACCEL is two-sided, so the product's most negative values are firms *decelerating* investment while levering up — a state the hypothesis does not claim is good — which contradicts the stated negative expected sign, and the indicator additionally piles roughly half the cross-section at exactly zero.

This is essentially the product of two well-published positive predictors (low investment/asset growth and net-cash or low-leverage financial soundness), both of which load directly on CMA and quality-type factors, so it reads as a repackaging of known anomalies whose FF5 alpha is likely largely spanned, and the "voluntary vs. forced" distinction is asserted rather than identified by the expression.

This is a near-mechanical restatement of the archive's ExternalFinancingGapLeverage (funding deficit × leverage) with input substitutions (ib for oancf, lt for dltt+dlc, plus aqc) that address a coverage constraint but change no economics, making it the kind of cosmetic variant the objective explicitly discourages — and swapping oancf for ib silently converts the "cash shortfall" leg into an accrual-contaminated earnings gap that overlaps the accruals anomaly.

Because sstk is zero or negligible for most firm-years, the second leg is empirically dominated by −oancf/at, so the composite collapses to high-investment × low-cash-profitability — i.e., a rediscovery of the CMA×RMW interaction and a close cousin of the archive's failed AccumulatedLossExpansionIntensity — and to the extent sstk does bind it simply re-tests the well-known net-share-issuance anomaly.

The maturity-mismatch channel (long-duration asset accumulation funded by net short-term claims) is economically distinct from the archive's level-of-leverage and funding-deficit signals, both legs are well-specified with high-coverage inputs, and the main risk — that negative net working capital often marks efficient, high-float business models rather than fragility — is a genuine empirical question rather than an internal inconsistency.

Asset-redeployability-conditioned distress cost is a legitimately different channel from anything in the archive and the sign is coherent, but Compustat intan is predominantly acquisition goodwill rather than the innovation-type intangibles the hypothesis invokes (making this partly a goodwill/serial-acquirer signal), and the claim that lt/(lt+ceq) avoids double-counting intangibles is wrong since ceq embeds them too.

The hiring-rate anomaly is well published and the sales-growth benchmark is a modest variant of existing "abnormal labor growth" measures, so the novelty rests entirely on the leverage interaction (combined operating-plus-financial leverage), which is a defensible but incremental cross-theme extension; emp coverage and its lumpy, annually-reported nature are the practical risks.

The self-benchmarked time-series capex shortfall is a genuinely different construction from the cross-sectional investment-level legs used elsewhere, but the expected negative sign runs directly against the dominant, well-documented low-investment premium that the first leg loads on, and the reasoning's explicit "if it comes out positive that's also informative" hedge signals weak ex-ante sign discipline.

The conditioner swap from stock leverage to near-term cash coverage is an economically distinct fragility channel and the sign logic is internally consistent, but the funding-gap leg is essentially the well-documented external-financing/free-cash-flow anomaly, so the incremental content rests entirely on whether the liquidity interaction survives controlling for the gap alone.

Both legs are identical to the archive's ExternalFinancingGapLeverage with only the accumulation window changed from one to three years — a cosmetic horizon variant rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the three-year sum of capex-minus-OCF is close to a rescaled version of cumulative asset/financing growth already known to predict returns.

The second-moment conditioner is a genuinely new channel in this archive and the sign is coherent, but earnings volatility is itself a documented standalone return predictor closely tied to idiosyncratic volatility and distress, so the test must show the product beats the volatility leg alone; a 5-year annual VOL will also thin coverage and lag badly.

The two legs are mechanically linked — growth in gross PP&E raises the denominator of sale/ppent and thus almost automatically produces a negative turnover delta — so the product is largely a nonlinear transform of capital/asset growth, which is a well-known published anomaly rather than a distinct capacity-utilization signal.

Replacing the intangible-collateral leg's leverage conditioner with cash coverage is a legitimate diagnosis-driven redesign rather than a cosmetic tweak, but COALESCE(gdwl,0) creates a large tied mass at zero so that for most firms the composite collapses to the cash-coverage leg alone, which should be reported as a diagnostic against the coverage-only benchmark.

This is the archive's ExternalFinancingGapLeverage with an industry z-score substituted for the raw leverage rank, and the switch to a signed conditioner silently changes the economics — high-deficit, below-industry-leverage firms are now pushed to the long leg, an implication the hypothesis never argues for and which contradicts the stated "penalize abnormal indebtedness" framing.

This is a mechanical recombination of two archive legs (the intan/at leg from SoftCollateralLeverage and the NEG(oancf/lt) leg from GoodwillStockWeakCashCoverage), and since Compustat `intan` is a superset containing `gdwl`, it is close to a broadened relabeling of the archive leader rather than a genuinely new mechanism.

Despite the disclaimer, this is a horizon variant of the archive's ReinvestmentAgainstDebtServiceCapacity (capx/ppent × NEG(oancf/lt)) — replacing one-year capex with a five-year sum in the same numerator over a closely related denominator will be highly correlated with the original, so the "vintage vs. flow" distinction it claims to test is not cleanly identified.

The expression is internally consistent and the tangible-net-worth conditioner is a defensible covenant-relevant reframing, though it algebraically reduces to a monotone function of (intan/at + lt/at), i.e. an additive version of the two legs already multiplied in SoftCollateralLeverage, so its incremental information over the archive is modest.

Replacing the goodwill stock with its three-year increment is a substantive stock-versus-flow decomposition of the archive leader with a clear diagnostic payoff (and it usefully assigns low signal values to firms that have already impaired), though the acquisition-flow leg overlaps with the known asset-growth/acquisition anomaly and with DebtFundedAcquisitionProgram.

The stated hypothesis is conditional ("among firms carrying heavy obligations") but the rank-product construction loads directly on the leverage main effect, so with a positive expected sign the signal is long high-leverage firms — precisely the exposure that has produced negative alphas in three archive signals — meaning a null result will be uninformative about investment smoothness.

The reasoning misdescribes the data — `txt` is total income tax expense including the deferred component, not cash taxes paid (`txpd`), so it is neither "hardest to manage upward" nor immune to accrual management — and the leg is in practice a scaled profitability proxy, making the signal a near-restatement of the well-known investment × low-profitability (CMA × RMW) interaction already present in the archive.

This is a one-term addition to the archive's existing TotalFundingRequirementBurden, and the added term (−che/at) makes the composite heavily a low-cash-holdings signal — a well-documented anomaly (Palazzo, cash-to-assets) — so any improvement is likely a rediscovery rather than evidence on the forced-external-financing mechanism, compounded by mixing a stock (che) with flows (capx, dlc, oancf) in one numerator.

Despite the claim that this is "not a recombination," it is exactly the product of two archive legs, and because the funding-requirement leg already contains −oancf it is economically near-collinear with GoodwillStockWeakCashCoverage (gdwl × weak cash coverage, ls_talpha −4.2), so a strong result would be uninformative about incremental mechanism.

The expression is internally inconsistent — wcap = act − lct already contains dlc inside lct, so subtracting wcap adds dlc back and double-counts maturing debt — and after that error the signal reduces mostly to capx/at minus working capital intensity, overlapping both the archive's MaturityMismatchedCapitalDeepening leg and the known net-operating-assets/working-capital anomalies.

Using the contemporaneous *flow* of current liabilities to identify who funded the capex is a genuinely distinct claim from the archive's level-based mismatch and gap signals and is well-formed, but the proposer should be aware that ΔlIct is a core component of Sloan accruals whose sign runs opposite to the hypothesized direction, so a null or positive result may simply reflect that offset rather than falsifying the maturity-mismatch story.

The second leg's natural direction contradicts the expected sign — shrinking book equity is dominated by repurchases and net equity retirement, which the issuance/composite-issuance anomaly says predicts *higher* returns — and in any case the construct is close in spirit to the already-tested AccumulatedLossExpansionIntensity (expansion × depleted equity base), which failed.

As an explicit identification control that swaps goodwill for its economic opposite while holding the cash-coverage leg fixed, this has real diagnostic value, though the coverage leg alone (oancf/lt) is a classic Beaver-style distress ratio so a strong negative result would mostly confirm the distress anomaly, and the stated EXPECTED_SIGN is asserted as negative even though the reasoning treats the sign as genuinely open.

This is a deflator swap on the archive's existing leader (TotalCashUsesRequirement) rather than a new mechanism, and because ppent+invt approaches zero for asset-light firms the ranked ratio will largely sort on inverse tangibility/intangible intensity — a channel the archive has already probed — so any improvement would be hard to attribute to borrowing-base capacity.

A clean, internally consistent leg-substitution diagnostic with a real coverage payoff, but note that capx + Δinvt − ib scaled by assets is close to the union of the published investment/asset-growth, inventory-growth and profitability anomalies, so an FF5-adjusted survival would need careful interpretation rather than being read as new evidence.

Accumulated-depreciation-to-gross-plant is a genuinely new stock construct in this archive and the "deferred replacement obligation versus voluntary discipline" framing is economically coherent and sign-consistent, though the reused NEG(oancf/lt) leg has already produced −0.03 to −0.055 alphas on its own, so the incremental contribution of the vintage leg must be shown rather than assumed.

Conditioning the funding requirement on leverage relative to the firm's own five-year maximum is a substantively different fragility concept (capacity exhaustion, not indebtedness level) that plausibly avoids the structural-leverage loading that undermined earlier variants, with the caveat that the bounded ratio piles a large mass at exactly 1.0 and may coarsen the conditioner's ranks.

Extending the mechanism to the labor margin is a reasonable and sign-consistent test, but the first leg is the published hiring-rate anomaly in raw form and the second leg is the archive's most-reused conditioner, so the signal risks being a known anomaly times an already-validated distress leg rather than new evidence.

The level-versus-innovation decomposition of the archive's strongest construct is a defensible diagnostic and correctly signed, but it is a standard own-history demeaning of an existing signal (and the INTERACTION_TYPE label "novel" is inaccurate — it is a time-series deviation, not an interaction), and comparable change-based legs in this archive have already failed.

This is a data-availability splice of two signals already in the archive (TotalCashUsesRequirement and EarningsBasedCashUses) with no new economic claim — the only difference is a missing-value convention, so any gain is a coverage patch rather than a testable mechanism.

The MIN operator's only incremental content relative to the strongest cash-based archive signal is a penalty of max(0, oancf − ib), i.e. it downgrades *low-accrual* firms, which runs against the direction of the well-published accruals anomaly, and because MIN requires both inputs the construct also forfeits the breadth the reasoning claims to exploit.

Adding acquisition outlays to the uses side is a modest but economically coherent respecification that the archive's goodwill results genuinely motivate, though it sits close to the published net-external-financing/total-investment anomaly and collapses to the existing leader for most non-acquirers, limiting the potential increment.

The two legs are conceptually distinct (size of the required raise versus convertibility of internal resources) and share no inputs, so this is a legitimate test of whether the inventory-illiquidity effect operates through the funding constraint rather than a repackaging of the oancf/lt coverage leg.

A three-year moving average of the archive's leading requirement signal is a mechanical smoothing variant, and since the level was already shown to dominate the innovation, the incremental information content of averaging a slow-moving state is minimal.

The conditioning leg RANK(NEG(oancf/lt)) has already been paired with five different partners in the archive with uniformly similar negative alphas, so this mostly re-tests that leg; moreover the stated justification is internally wrong — aqc is zero for most firms, so the composition ratio has exactly the tied-zero mass the reasoning claims to avoid, and it is unstable when capx+aqc is near zero or aqc is negative.

This is a mechanical splice of two archive winners (TotalCorporateCashUses and RequirementWithSlowingInventoryTurns) with no new economic content, and it double-counts inventory (Δinvt inside the uses leg, invt/sale in the conditioner), so any gain over the existing t=−3.59 version would be uninterpretable and almost certainly within noise of the parent signals.

The proposal openly concedes it "isolates the measurement question rather than the economic one" — averaging two already-tested inventory conditioners (t=−4.25 and t=−3.59) into a SUMRANK is a cosmetic variant of both parents, and a composite of two correlated inventory ratios cannot discriminate the mechanism it claims to test.

This is the exact intersection of two existing archive signals — PeerRelativeFundingRequirement and TotalCorporateCashUses — differing only by the addition of the aqc term inside an already-tested IND_RANK, which is too trivial an increment to warrant a separate test; the industry-neutrality argument would have justified the peer-relative version, which has already been run.

The capex-stripping test is a legitimate discriminating experiment against the CMA/asset-growth (Cooper-Gulen-Schill) spanning concern that plausibly explains the whole capex-containing family, but the resulting expression is close to inventory growth interacted with inventory-turnover deterioration — i.e., near the published inventory-growth anomaly (Belo-Lin) — so a positive result should be read as mechanism identification rather than a new signal.

This is the most economically distinct proposal in the batch — the two legs share no inputs and it substitutes an operating-cost-rigidity conditioner for the archive's over-recycled oancf/lt ratio — though the reviewer should be prepared to attribute any result partly to the known standalone hiring-rate anomaly (Belo-Lin-Bazdresch) rather than to the conjunction.

Substituting ib for oancf to lift coverage from ~0.08 to ~0.12 is a defensible robustness test of the archive's binding sparse-sample weakness rather than a pure performance chase, but it remains a recombination of two existing signals and should be judged on whether the wide-sample result is comparable, not on whether it happens to score higher.

This is a mechanical splice of two archived signals — the ib-for-oancf substitution already run in BroadSampleRequirementSlowingTurns applied to the already-tested RequirementWithAbnormalInventoryOverhang — so it is a cosmetic coverage variant rather than a substantively different construction, and its "success criterion" (results comparable to the narrow sample) is almost guaranteed given the two legs are unchanged in economic content.

The expression is internally inconsistent with its hypothesis: multiplying a signed level requirement by a signed IND_ADJ amplifier makes the product positive for cash-generative firms with below-peer inventory (negative × negative), placing exactly the healthiest firms at the short end, which is the opposite of the stated economics and is not fixed by winsorizing.

SUMRANK of two amplifiers already tested separately against the identical requirement leg is a blend rather than a new mechanism, and because equal-weight rank averaging dilutes whichever leg is stronger, the near-certain outcome is a result bracketed by the two constituents that adjudicates nothing.

Deteriorating sales-per-employee is a genuinely distinct conditioner from headcount growth, the stated motivation (disentangling operating-cost rigidity from the published labor-hiring anomaly) is a real identification concern, and expression and expected sign are consistent — though note DELTA(sale/emp) is partly mechanically driven by emp growth, so overlap with the hiring version should be checked directly.

Industry-relative inventory-to-sales as a standalone predictor is essentially the published inventory-level/inventory-growth anomaly (Thomas–Zhang, Belo–Lin) and is a single trivial ratio, but the ablation logic is sound and the run is cheap, so it should be treated as a diagnostic benchmark rather than as a candidate signal.

The economic story is about trade credit but the proxy is total current liabilities, which is dominated by short-term debt and accruals — so a falling lct/sale can equally mean the firm repaid revolver debt (a good outcome) — and it mechanically overlaps the dlc term in the requirement leg and with the working-capital accrual anomaly; use ap directly if the supplier-credit channel is the intended mechanism.

A defensible hybrid of the archive's two strongest constructions (dollarized budget-identity inclusion plus own-history benchmarking) rather than a rank splice, though it is close to the boundary of a variant-of-a-variant and the SUB(x, TS_MIN(x,5)) term is non-negative by construction so it partly proxies inventory-ratio volatility rather than a directional build.

This is the archive's leading signal (RequirementWithSelfBenchmarkedOverhang) with TS_RANK swapped for its cardinal analogue — a measurement-scale tweak that, after cross-sectional RANK is applied, will be highly correlated with the original and therefore constitutes a cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different hypothesis.

A legitimate and clearly motivated sample-robustness test of the leading signal that materially raises coverage, but it is a robustness re-run rather than a new mechanism, and the requirement already contains DELTA(invt,1) while the conditioner is also inventory-based, so part of the interaction is self-referential.

The expression matches the hypothesis (high emp/sale relative to own history = overstaffing, high signal, negative expected return), the labor margin is economically distinct from the working-capital margin, and the own-history benchmark plausibly separates it from the published hiring-rate and labor-productivity anomalies.

Internally consistent and completes a coherent three-margin test of the overhang concept, but ppent/sale relative to own history is largely driven by declining sales and thus overlaps existing capacity-utilization and asset-turnover measures, making it the weakest-differentiated of the three template ports.

The sign and construction are correct (low cash-to-current-liabilities by the firm's own five-year standard maps to a high signal value and negative expected returns), and using the own-history benchmark is a genuine diagnosis-driven fix for the earlier cash-buffer conditioners that failed on the FMB slope while also reducing overlap with the published cash-holdings anomaly.
